text: In the last lesson you learned that correlation measures how tightly two variables move together, and never proves cause. Simple linear regression takes the next step — it fits a straight line through the data so you can describe the relationship in concrete units and make predictions. It's also the foundation of most of the machine learning you'll meet later in this program.

Simple linear regression assumes an outcome y is roughly a straight-line function of a predictor x, plus noise — y equals b-zero plus b-one times x, plus error. b-zero is the intercept, b-one is the slope. Least squares picks the b-zero and b-one that make the sum of squared residuals as small as possible, where a residual is the vertical gap between an actual value and the line.

Using 60 illustrative homes, size in square feet and price in thousands of dollars: scipy's linregress gives a slope of 0.1493 and an intercept of 45.16, with R-squared of 0.944. linregress returns the slope, intercept, correlation, a p-value for the slope, and the slope's standard error.

The formulas are short enough to write by hand — the slope is how x and y vary together, divided by how much x varies alone; the intercept is chosen so the line passes through the point of means. Computing it directly gives the exact same 0.1493 and 45.16 — there's no magic hiding in the library.

Reading the output: the slope, 0.1493, means each additional square foot goes with about 149 dollars of extra price. The intercept, 45.16, is the predicted price at zero square feet — not meaningful here, since no house has zero area; intercepts are often just an anchor for the line.

R-squared, 0.944, means about 94 percent of the variation in price is accounted for by size — in simple regression it equals the correlation squared. Residuals always average zero; their spread, about 22.8 thousand here, is the typical size of a miss. Plot them — a curve or a funnel shape means a straight line is the wrong model.

A 2,000 square foot home is predicted at about 343.7 thousand dollars. The 95 percent confidence interval for the slope runs roughly from 0.140 to 0.159, built with the standard error and a t critical value with n minus 2 degrees of freedom. The p-value tests whether the true slope is actually zero.

Three cautions. Don't extrapolate — the line is only supported by the range of x you actually observed; a 10,000 square foot mansion may follow a completely different pattern. Association, not causation — the slope describes how price differs across homes of different sizes, it doesn't prove adding a room raises any specific home's value.

And always look at residuals and outliers — one extreme point can pull the whole line. To recap: least squares fits the line that minimizes squared residuals. The slope is the change in y per unit of x, R-squared is the share of variation explained, and residuals show whether the line actually fits. Next: designing an A/B test properly, before you ever look at the results.
